scenes.title: A matrix is a vector with dimensions
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: R matrices are atomic vectors with a two-dimensional dim attribute.
The first subscript is the row and the second is the column. R uses one-based indexing.
matrix() fills down columns by default; byrow=TRUE changes the fill direction.

ask.q: What is the key output rule to check in this section?
ask.nudge: Identify dimensions, fill direction or operator semantics before calculating.

items.recall: The number of rows followed by the number of columns.
refresh: dim(A) returns a length-two integer vector: first the row count, then the column count. For a matrix with three rows and two columns, dim(A) is c(3,2).
Always keep the order straight when reading dimensions. nrow(A) and ncol(A) report the two values separately, while dim(A) reports both together in row-column order.
In R, the operator %*% performs matrix multiplication. The ordinary * operator multiplies corresponding entries and is not a substitute for a matrix product.
Before using %*%, check that the number of columns in the left matrix equals the number of rows in the right matrix. If those inner dimensions differ, the product is not conformable.

items.recall: It returns the transpose of A.
refresh: The transpose exchanges rows and columns. A matrix with r rows and c columns becomes a matrix with c rows and r columns.
When tracing matrix expressions, write the dimensions before and after transposition. This makes it easier to check whether a later matrix product is defined and what dimensions its result will have.

scenes.title: Construction and column-major filling
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: matrix(1:6,nrow=2,ncol=3) produces rows (1,3,5) and (2,4,6).
The input vector is consumed down the first column, then down the next column.
Use byrow=TRUE only when the requested layout is row-wise.

scenario.title: A researcher's data layout
body: A researcher creates a matrix from six measurements. Default matrix construction fills down columns, so the first two observations occupy the first column of a two-row matrix.
If the intended layout is row-wise, the researcher must set byrow=TRUE.

The analyst should also record the dimensions of each intermediate object, not merely the final answer. This makes it possible to identify a non-conformable product before attempting arithmetic and to distinguish a matrix product from elementwise multiplication. In an examination setting, writing the inner dimensions first is a quick way to avoid a common operator error.
scenario.q: What is the first row of matrix(1:6,nrow=2)?

scenes.title: Dimensions and indexing
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: dim(A) returns c(nrow(A),ncol(A)).
A[i,j] selects one element; A[i,] selects row i; A[,j] selects column j.
Use drop=FALSE to keep a one-row or one-column subset as a matrix.

scenes.title: Operator meanings
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: A*B multiplies corresponding entries element by element.
A%*%B performs matrix multiplication using row-by-column dot products.
t(A) transposes; det(A) calculates a determinant; solve(A,b) solves Ax=b.

scenes.title: Element-wise arithmetic versus matrix product
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: The * operator is element-wise; it does not perform a linear-algebra product.
For A of size m×n and B of size p×q, A%*%B exists only when n=p.
The resulting product has size m×q.

scenes.title: Transpose, determinant and inverse
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: t(A) exchanges rows and columns: an m×n matrix becomes n×m.
For [[a,b],[c,d]], det(A)=ad−bc. The determinant requires a square matrix.
solve(A,b) solves Ax=b; solve(A) gives the inverse when A is nonsingular.

scenario.title: A statistician checks invertibility
body: A statistician is given a 2×2 matrix and needs to decide whether it has an inverse before solving a system.
The determinant is computed first. A nonzero determinant indicates that the square matrix is nonsingular.

The analyst should also record the dimensions of each intermediate object, not merely the final answer. This makes it possible to identify a non-conformable product before attempting arithmetic and to distinguish a matrix product from elementwise multiplication. In an examination setting, writing the inner dimensions first is a quick way to avoid a common operator error.
scenario.q: What does a nonzero determinant establish?
scenario.answer: The matrix is nonsingular and invertible.

scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: diag(A) extracts diagonal entries; diag(n) creates an n×n identity matrix.
rowSums(A) and colSums(A) calculate row and column totals.
For [[1,2],[3,4]], rowSums is (3,7), colSums is (4,6), and diag is (1,4).

scenes.title: Read a matrix expression
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: If A is 2×3, then t(A) is 3×2.
The product t(A)%*%A has dimensions (3×2)(2×3), so it is 3×3.
A%*%t(A) instead has dimensions (2×3)(3×2), so it is 2×2.

solution.why: Transposition exchanges the row and column dimensions.
The inner dimensions match and the outer dimensions determine the result.
Matrix multiplication is order-sensitive; reversing the factors changes the result dimensions.

scenes.title: Exam traps
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: Default matrix filling is column-wise, not row-wise.
* is element-wise and %*% is matrix multiplication.
Matrix multiplication requires matching inner dimensions; det() requires a square matrix.
Use drop=FALSE when a selected row or column must remain a matrix.

scenes.title: Matrix operator quick sheet
scenes.objective: Interpret R matrix construction, dimensions and operators.
body: matrix() fills columns unless byrow=TRUE. Index as row, column.
A*B is element-wise; A%*%B is matrix multiplication with matching inner dimensions.
t() swaps dimensions; det() requires square matrices; solve(A,b) solves Ax=b.
diag(), rowSums() and colSums() extract or summarise matrix structure.
